records.name_note: Ocimum basilicum is the currently accepted binomial for sweet basil. The RHS lists Ocimum album and Ocimum thyrsiflorum as synonyms filed under Ocimum basilicum (not the other direction), and every other cited source (NC State, Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, Penn State, University of Maryland) uses Ocimum basilicum directly, so no name correction is warranted.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox tags this species "non-toxic for cats" and "non-toxic for dogs"; no admissible source reports a toxic compound or symptom for pets.
unknowns: light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source gives footcandle light values for basil; sources describe sun in duration/exposure terms only.
direct_sun_hours_max: sources state a minimum of 6-8 hours full sun; none state an upper limit, so left null.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source states basil's ambient humidity preference (only that high humidity favors downy mildew disease, not a stated need).

day_f_min / day_f_max: Clemson and Penn State describe transplant-timing temperatures only in decade terms ('70s', '80s') without a precise number pair, so not populated to avoid inventing exact endpoints.

night_f_min / night_f_max: Clemson states nighttime above 50°F while Penn State Extension states night above 60°F for similar but distinct transplant/move-outside guidance; two admissible sources conflict, so left null rather than arbitrarily choosing one.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source discusses a dormancy or cool-rest period; basil is grown as a warm-season annual with no rest phase described.

water_dry_down_target / water_check_depth_cm / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a watering-frequency day count, soil-check depth, or dry-down target for basil.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_strength / fertilize_active_months: Clemson describes a one-time granular 5-10-10 application before planting plus an optional calcium-nitrate side-dress about two months later -- a planting-triggered schedule, not a recurring interval or houseplant liquid-fertilizer strength, so it does not map to these fields.

soil_base: sources describe both garden soil ('rich, well-drained soil') and container potting mix with no specific categorical potting-mix name given, so left null rather than guessing between garden_bed and standard_potting.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: The number (40) matches the quote, but the quote is about the wrong subject. The Penn State 'Basil: A Summer Favorite' source reads in full: 'When cold weather is predicted, be sure to harvest all basil. Temperatures below 40°F will discolor leaves, which is why stems of basil picked for use in the kitchen are best held in a glass of water at room temperature instead of in the refrigerator.' This is post-harvest storage advice for cut stems (don't refrigerate harvested basil), not a statement about the chilling-injury threshold of the living, rooted plant in a garden or as a houseplant — which is what chill_damage_f is meant to capture (it sits alongside day_f/night_f/cool_rest_note, all live-plant environmental fields). No admissible source in the record gives a numeric chill-damage threshold for the growing plant; the only other cold-related citations (MOBOT 'Intolerant of frost', UMD 'not tolerant of chilly temperatures', RHS H1c ~5-10°C) are all qualitative and were correctly NOT used for this field. Using the cut-stem-refrigeration number here overreaches on context.

soil_ph_min — removed on audit: The Clemson quote used ('bring the soil pH to between 6.0 and 6.5') is truncated right before the source's own qualifying sentence: 'This is also the best pH range for most vegetables.' Clemson is not reporting a basil-specific optimum — it is giving the generic vegetable-garden liming target and noting explicitly that it applies to 'most vegetables' generally, not basil in particular. This is a class-level ('most vegetables') figure presented as a species-specific value, the exact failure pattern the audit is meant to catch. No other admissible source in the record gives a numeric pH range for basil.

soil_ph_max — removed on audit: Same defect as soil_ph_min: the 6.0–6.5 figure comes from Clemson's generic 'best pH range for most vegetables' liming advice, not a basil-specific pH requirement, and the quote in the record stops just short of the sentence that discloses this.

water_regime — removed on audit: The record stores an unqualified water_regime: "keep_moist", but its own cited RHS quote (verified verbatim against the live page) gives three different answers depending on context: newly planted chives need watering during dry spells; established in-ground chives "shouldn't need any additional watering – except during exceptionally prolonged dry spells" (i.e. drought-tolerant once established); and only container-grown chives should be watered "to keep the compost evenly moist." The record picked the container-only reading and presented it as the general field value. Since the record also carries outdoor_sun_exposure (full_sun/part_shade), in-ground/garden growing is clearly in scope, not just pots — so a reader of the stored value alone gets blanket "keep moist" guidance that directly contradicts the source's explicit statement for the established in-ground case, risking overwatering. The caveat is disclosed only in the citation's parenthetical, not in the value itself.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The record sets soil_drainage to 'moderate', but the only citation supporting it quotes Penn State Extension: 'Full sun; rich, moist but not constantly wet, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.5.' The source's own word for drainage is 'well-drained,' not 'moderate' — and this is corroborated by RHS's separate moisture note for the same species ('Well-drained soil'). No cited source describes dill's drainage need as 'moderate'; the researcher silently recategorized 'well-drained' into a different bucket ('moderate') that the quote does not support and that arguably understates the drainage the sources actually call for.

night_f_min — removed on audit: The value 45 comes from Penn State's line that dill 'is best sown directly outdoors ... when the night temperature is above 45°F' — a seed-sowing/planting-timing recommendation about safe germination conditions, not a statement about the minimum night temperature a growing or established dill plant needs or tolerates. The claim label itself concedes this scope ('minimum night temperature recommended before sowing dill seed outdoors'), yet the number was still written into a general night_f_min field. This is in tension with the record's own other citation from NC State ('Dill plants can survive low temperatures'), which suggests mature dill tolerates temperatures below the sowing threshold. A germination-timing guideline is being used to stand in for a general cold-tolerance figure the sources don't actually give — the same gap the record correctly left open for chill_damage_f.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: Value 20 is sourced only from MOBOT's "Leaves remain harvestable until temperatures drop into the low 20s F." (verified live on plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=276060). "Low 20s" is a fuzzy range (~20-23F), not a literal '20' -- the number in the claim label is not literally present in the quote, which the audit instructions flag as a refutable defect regardless of whether 20 is roughly in the right neighborhood. The quote also describes a harvestability/palatability cutoff ('leaves remain harvestable'), not an explicit tissue-damage threshold, so equating it 1:1 with a 'chill_damage_f' figure over-reads the source.

soil_base — removed on audit: The only citation, NC State's "Parsley prefers consistently moist, well-drained rich soil in full sun or light shade" (verified verbatim on plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/petroselinum-crispum/), is a pure soil-texture/moisture description and never mentions garden beds, in-ground planting, or location at all. The same NC State page's own 'Landscape Location' field lists Container, Hanging Baskets, and Houseplants alongside Patio, and RHS/Clemson both treat containers as an equally standard way to grow parsley (including for overwintering), so nothing in the cited quote actually supports singling out 'garden_bed' as the base growing context over a container/potting scenario.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: All three supporting citations describe outdoor container/patio garden use or a temporary overwintering technique, not indoor houseplant suitability. NC State's quote is pulled from its 'Landscape Location' attribute list (Coastal, Container, Patio, Small Space, Walkways) -- an outdoor-garden-design category, not an indoor-growing recommendation. RHS's quote is likewise from 'Suggested planting locations and garden types' (City and courtyard gardens, Cottage garden, Patio and container plants, Gravel garden, Wall side borders) -- again outdoor garden types. The UMD quote ('Cuttings can be taken in late summer, rooted and potted up and moved indoors to a sunny location. Replant outdoors after the danger of frost has past.') describes a seasonal overwintering technique for propagated cuttings, explicitly followed by replanting outdoors -- not a claim that the species is well-suited to being grown as a houseplant. None of the three cited sources states that Salvia officinalis thrives or is recommended as an indoor houseplant; the record conflates 'can be grown in an outdoor pot/patio container' and 'cuttings can be wintered indoors temporarily' with 'is_houseplant.' This is compounded by the species' own stated requirement of full sun (6+ hours direct), which is difficult to supply indoors, making the 'true' designation actively misleading for indoor-care guidance.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The cited Missouri Botanical Garden quote is 'Easily grown in average, medium moisture, well-drained soils in full sun to light shade.' That sentence names two distinct soil attributes: a moisture-retention descriptor ('medium moisture') and a drainage-rate descriptor ('well-drained soils'). The record's soil_drainage field is set to 'moderate', which reads as though it was derived from the 'medium moisture' phrase rather than from the sentence's actual drainage statement, which is unambiguously 'well-drained' (i.e., fast/good drainage), not a moderate/average drainage rate. Every other source touching on drainage in this record's own citation set agrees with 'well-drained,' not 'moderate': the Clemson quote for outdoor_sun_exposure says 'rich, well-drained soil,' and the RHS quotes say 'free-draining conditions' / 'free-draining soil' / 'dislikes soggy conditions.' Verified directly against the live MoBot page (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid=275984, confirmed to be the Coriandrum sativum 'Slo-Bolt' entry) — the quote text matches verbatim, so this is a labeling/mapping error, not a fabricated quote: the researcher appears to have conflated the moisture-retention descriptor with the drainage-rate field the value was actually supposed to represent.

toxic_to_pets — removed on audit: The record's accepted taxon is Origanum vulgare (the straight species), and every other field in this record is sourced from NC State's species-level page (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/origanum-vulgare/). I fetched that exact page and its 'Problems' field reads only: 'Root rot may occur in wet, poorly drained soils. Watch for fungal diseases. Aphids, leaf miners and spider mites may appear.' -- no cat/dog/horse tag at all. Missouri Botanical Garden's species-level page (already cited elsewhere in this record for soil/sun) likewise lists Problems as only 'Root rot... fungal diseases... Aphids, leaf miners and spider mites' with no animal-toxicity tag. The 'Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses' tags used to justify toxic_to_pets=true come from a DIFFERENT, separately-curated NC State plant record for Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum (a distinct URL: .../origanum-vulgare-subsp-hirtum/), which is a specific cultivated subspecies, not the species itself. NC State evidently curates Problems independently per taxon page (the species page omits what the subspecies page includes), so importing the subspecies' tag onto the species record is exactly the kind of species/subspecies-mismatch transfer the audit is meant to catch -- one taxonomic rank more specific than the classic genus-to-species error, but the same failure mode. I also confirmed via a direct fetch that NC State's page nowhere defines what 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses' even means (no glossary/tooltip text), so even on its home page the tag is an unglossed category link, not a substantiated toxicity claim.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Same root defect as toxic_to_pets: this text is built entirely on the subsp. hirtum page's bare 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses' tags, which do not appear on the species-level (Origanum vulgare) page that is otherwise this record's authoritative NC State source. The detail text's own admission that 'No toxic compound, symptoms, or severity are given on the page' is accurate as a description of that subspecies page, but it does not rescue the underlying claim -- it is a bare, undefined category tag for a different taxon than the one this record represents, not evidence of toxicity for Origanum vulgare the species.

water_dry_down_target — removed on audit: The cited Penn State Extension quote ('Once established, oregano requires little water... wait until the soil dries out between waterings') is real, but the record's added parenthetical scope -- '(established, in-ground or potted plants)' -- overreaches it. I fetched the same Penn State page and it explicitly distinguishes container care: 'Plants in pots require some supplemental irrigation,' as a separate statement from the in-ground 'requires little water' guidance. The source itself treats potted-plant watering as materially different from the in-ground drought-tolerant case; the citation's quote never mentions containers, so folding 'potted plants' into the dry-down target as if the same source endorsed it for both contexts is an unsupported extrapolation -- notable because this is a houseplant-flagged record (is_houseplant=true) where the container case is exactly the one likely to be acted on.

name_note — removed on audit: The name_note attributes the quote 'a robust but relatively common plant... seldom sold for a specific ornamental or culinary use' to 'NC State Extension.' I fetched NC State's origanum-vulgare page directly and searched it for this phrase -- it does not appear anywhere on that page. The phrase is instead verbatim text from the Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder page (plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=281411), under its 'Noteworthy Characteristics' section: 'The straight species is a robust but relatively common plant that is, as a general rule, seldom sold for a specific ornamental or culinary use.' This is a straightforward source misattribution -- citing NC State for a claim that is actually MBG's. The second half of the note (subsp. hirtum described on NC State's page as 'Greek oregano: the standard culinary oregano') is correctly attributed and verified present in NC State's Cultivars/Varieties section.

water_regime — removed on audit: The value 'dry_thoroughly_between' is a specific watering methodology, but its NC State citation ('It is frost and drought-tolerant.') only states a survivability trait -- that the plant CAN survive drought -- not a care instruction about letting the medium dry out thoroughly before rewatering. That is the classic 'sounds related but doesn't actually state this value' failure: drought-tolerant plants can still be recommended for light/frequent watering elsewhere; tolerance of drought is not the same claim as a prescribed dry-down-then-water-thoroughly regime. The companion RHS citation is meaningfully stronger (explicit root-rot-from-dampness warning, 'rarely needs watering') but is still an inference to the specific labeled cadence rather than a literal statement of it, and it describes outdoor/garden thyme rather than the container/houseplant context the record separately asserts (is_houseplant: true). Because one of the two supporting citations doesn't actually support the claim and the field is flagged as high-stakes, the field should be treated as unsound as sourced.

soil_ph_max — removed on audit: The NC State quote is two separate categorical tags on the page -- 'Alkaline (>8.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' -- not a single continuous range statement. The '>8.0' tag means the source considers pH above 8.0 ALSO tolerated (an open-ended/unbounded category), yet the claim converts that same number into a hard ceiling of exactly 8.0. The digit '8.0' does appear in the quote, but not in the role assigned to it -- it marks the bottom of a further-tolerated alkaline range, not the top of the plant's tolerance. Presenting it as soil_ph_max therefore understates what the source itself says the plant tolerates and isn't literally asserted by the quote.

normalizations: 2026-08-19: landed with zero loader-found defects, unlike b6. The research and audit prompts were tightened after b6's two findings -- auditors were told explicitly to re-derive every label number from its own quote, and to distinguish a 'safe to eat' (human/culinary) claim from a 'safe for pets' claim. Chives correctly resolved toxic_to_pets true (N-propyl disulfide, UF/IFAS, species explicitly named) despite being a kitchen herb -- the scenario the prompt change targeted.
